newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S., France said agreed on Bosnia envoy.
newsitem.headline: U.S., France said agreed on Bosnia envoy.

text.p: The United States and France have agreed that Carlos Westendorp, Spain's ambassador to the United Nations, should be the next international envoy to Bosnia, diplomatic sources said Monday.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, after talks with her French counterpart, acknowledged agreement on the issue but refused to identify the individual. However, diplomatic sources told Reuters: "Westendorp is right."

The United States has been pushing for American Jacques Klein, U.N. administrator for the difficult situation in Croatia's disputed eastern Slavonia region, to be Westendorp's deputy and officials said a consensus was forming around that appointment.
They said, though, that a second deputy may be named and that a European would fill that role.

The major western powers involved in Bosnia peace efforts -- the United States, France, Germany, Russia and Britain -- were expected to appoint Westendorp during a meeting on Friday in Sintra, Portugal.
He would succeed Swedish diplomat Carl Bildt who for months has delayed leaving the post because the major powers could not agree on a replacement.
One of Albright's main goals on a week-long trip to Europe, including the Balkans, is to push a U.S. initiative for more aggressive peace efforts in Bosnia.

The 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton accords ended war there but there are increasing concerns that efforts to secure the peace by building a unified Bosnia are foundering because of lingering hostilities among rival factions, resistance to integration and lack of cooperation in bringing war criminals to trial.

Although some have expressed concern that Westendorp is not high-powered enough to handle Bosnia's rival factions, one U.S. official said: "He is the consensus choice. He's got a very good reputation. He's got the support of European governments."

Albright discussed the U.S. initiative during talks with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and afterwards State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters there was broad agreement between Washington and Paris on Bosnia.
This includes the need to strengthen the civilian components of the Dayton peace accords such as increased training for an independent civilian police force.

But Burns said the two countries remain at odds over the multi-million dollar U.S. programme to train and equip the army of Bosnia's Croat-Moslem federation, which Washington insists is needed to equalise a Bosnian Serb superiority in arms.

At a brief news conference after their meeting, Albright and de Charette made a special effort to praise the current state of U.S.-French relations, which under former Secretary of State Warren Christopher had become quite fractious and nasty.
De Charette said the quality of bilateral ties was "very very high and that is due in large part to the personal qualities" of Albright.
Albright, a multi-linguist, conducted the meeting entirely in French, the first time in recent history that an American secretary of state has done so, Burns said.

Albright was later to have a private dinner with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov. As in the meeting with de Charette, those talks were to cover NATO enlargement, the NATO-Russia security accord to be signed on Tuesday and Bosnia.

As part of the U.S. initiative, Albright announced last week that U.S. troops, the bulk of the NATO-led stabilisation force in Bosnia (SFOR), would take on new roles in helping ensure the safe return of war refugees and newly elected local officials and also establish telecommunications links among Bosnia's still-hostile ethnic Moslem, Croat and Serb communities.

In addition, she said, Washington would bring increased financial and other pressures to bear to encourage parties to the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accords -- including Croatia and Serbia as well as the Bosnian factions -- to meet their commitments.

Many experts see a deepening crisis in Bosnia, with the country ultimately being partitioned. Albright said last week that Washington remained committed to a unified state with two entities, one for Serbs and the other a Moslem-Croat federation.
